payload.executive_summary: This candidate implements a “Foundation First” plan for a Markdown-to-static-site generator using the plugin-based build core (O2). The approach invests upfront in a stable plugin API, a shared build-context data model, and deterministic build orchestration, then delivers core features (rendering, links/backlinks, tags, search) as independently testable plugins. This sequencing prioritizes long-term maintainability and extensibility while explicitly addressing key early risks: convention ambiguity (links/tags), scaling constraints for indexing/search, XSS/content handling, and the critical privacy leakage risk (K8) via a mandatory build-time safeguard.

architecture_choice.rationale: A plugin-based core best matches the branch’s “Foundation First” posture: it reduces long-term coupling between ingestion, analysis (links/tags), rendering, and search, while enabling thin-slice delivery of features as swappable plugins once a stable shared data model and lifecycle are established. This directly supports requirements that benefit from clear separations (R1/R3 ingestion vs. R9/R10 graph vs. R7/R8 search vs. R2 static emission), and it front-loads mitigation of the highest architectural risks (API instability, data model mistakes, and privacy leakage K8) by making these explicit early design artifacts and contract tests.
architecture_choice.high_level_dataflow: CLI invokes the Core Build Engine, which loads configuration and registers plugins. Lifecycle execution proceeds deterministically: (1) ingest plugins discover .md files and populate the Shared Build Context with canonical Note records; (2) transform plugins enrich notes with parsed metadata/tags and a resolved link graph with backlinks; (3) render plugins convert Markdown to HTML and generate site pages (notes, tags index, per-tag pages, navigation); (4) search plugin builds and emits a client-side index artifact; (5) emit plugin writes all HTML/CSS/JS/static assets and report artifacts to the output directory with base-path handling. The browser then loads static pages and the shipped search index to execute search fully client-side.

milestones.name: Intake → Generate: Foundation specification (plugin API + shared data model + determinism/security baselines)

deliverables.text: Plugin lifecycle spec for hooks (ingest/transform/render/emit), plugin dependency declaration, and deterministic ordering rules.
Shared Build Context schema: canonical NoteId strategy, required fields (raw markdown, front matter, derived metadata), and link-graph representation (forward links + backlinks).
Security & privacy baseline spec: raw-HTML handling default, template escaping expectations, and the proposed K8 build-time safeguard behavior.
Open-questions resolution plan for blockers (Q1/Q2/Q3/Q4/Q10) with explicit defaults/assumptions and HITL sign-off points.

exit_criteria: Lifecycle and data-model contracts are written down and reviewed for stability impact (plugin API versioning expectations and backward-compatibility policy).
Deterministic build requirements are specified (stable ordering, no timestamps by default, locale/timezone controls).
Security boundary defaults are selected (raw HTML policy) and flagged for required HITL approval where applicable.
Blocker questions are either answered or explicitly gated with safe defaults and documented limitations.

milestones.name: Generate: Core engine + CLI orchestration (minimal end-to-end build skeleton)

deliverables.text: CLI build command implementing required arguments (input dir, output dir) and clear error reporting (R5, R6).
Core Build Engine that loads plugins, enforces deterministic ordering, and executes lifecycle hooks against a shared Build Context (O2 core).
Ingestion plugin implementing recursive discovery of .md files and creation of Note records in the shared context (R1).
Emit plugin that writes static artifacts to output directory and produces a build summary/report artifact (R2, R6).

exit_criteria: AT1, AT5, and AT6 pass for the skeleton pipeline (discovery, CLI invocation, and actionable failures).
End-to-end build produces a static output directory (even if content is placeholder) and is reproducible across repeated runs (ordering stable).

milestones.name: Generate: Markdown rendering + theming (per-note HTML pages + global navigation shell)

deliverables.text: Markdown Render plugin producing CommonMark-compliant HTML and preserving standard Markdown structures (R3, R4), with an explicit raw-HTML policy.
Theme/Template plugin generating per-note pages with consistent layout and a minimal global navigation shell (supporting R17 as a SHOULD).
Static asset packaging (CSS/JS) ensuring the output remains fully static and browser-loadable (R2, R14).

exit_criteria: AT2, AT3, and AT4 pass for a representative fixture set (static-only output, per-note page generation, formatting fidelity).
Template layer consistently escapes user-controlled strings per security baseline (no direct injection paths).

milestones.name: Generate: Link resolution/backlinks + tags as thin-slice plugins (core navigation features)

deliverables.text: Link Resolution & Backlink plugin supporting standard Markdown relative links and generating backlinks sections per note (R9, R10), with broken-link warning behavior aligned to R18 (SHOULD).
Metadata & Tag Extraction plugin supporting at least one configured tagging convention and tag normalization rules (R11, R16), attaching tags to notes in the shared context.
Tag pages generation (tags index + per-tag pages) with tag links rendered on each note page (R12, R13).

exit_criteria: AT9 and AT10 pass (links resolve to generated HTML; backlinks list correct sources and are clickable).
AT11, AT12, and AT13 pass (tags extracted, displayed, and tag pages generated correctly).
Unresolved links produce warnings with actionable context and do not crash the build by default (targeting R18).

milestones.name: Validate → Review: Search + hardening (performance, cross-browser, security/privacy safeguards)

deliverables.text: Search Index plugin generating a build-time search index artifact and client-side search runtime integration (R7, R8), including a size/performance report keyed to target scale (Q3).
Cross-browser validation runbook and results for core flows (navigation, search, backlinks, tags) on Chrome/Firefox/Safari/Edge (R14).
Security hardening: XSS/content-injection tests and enforcement of raw-HTML/template escaping policy (mitigating K7).

Privacy leakage safeguard implementation for notes marked private (K8): mandatory build-time check + explicit user override mechanism, and confirmation that private notes are excluded from outputs/search by default unless override is provided.

exit_criteria: AT7 and AT8 pass (search runs fully client-side; index artifact is produced and loaded from static output).
AT14 passes across target browsers with no JS errors that block core functionality.
Security/privacy safeguards are validated and explicitly signed off per governance posture (high HITL strictness).

decision_log.question: Which architecture option should be used as the core implementation approach?
decision_log.choice: Adopt O2: a plugin-based build core with a defined lifecycle and a shared build context.
decision_log.rationale: The project’s feature set naturally decomposes into ingest, transform (links/tags), render, search, and emit responsibilities. A plugin architecture enables a stable foundation-first core while allowing subsequent features to ship as thin-slice plugins with isolated testing, aligning with the branch’s emphasis on reducing architectural risk and technical debt.
alternatives_considered: O1 monolithic CLI pipeline
O3 build on an existing static site generator
O4 multi-stage pipeline with intermediate artifacts
what_would_change_this_decision: If time-to-first-feature is the dominant priority over extensibility and long-term maintainability, O1 could be preferred.
If incremental builds/watch mode is a primary requirement early, O4 or an SSG-based approach (O3) may offer faster leverage.
If the project scope is expected to remain small and stable (no plugin ecosystem), the extra complexity of O2 may not be justified.

evidence_pointers.note: O2 describes the plugin-based core with lifecycle hooks and a shared build context.

decision_log.question: What plugin lifecycle and ordering model will the core engine enforce?
decision_log.choice: Use a fixed lifecycle (ingest → transform → render → emit) with deterministic plugin ordering and explicit dependency declarations.
decision_log.rationale: A fixed lifecycle reduces non-obvious coupling and makes debugging predictable, while explicit dependencies and deterministic ordering mitigate non-deterministic builds (K20) and plugin-conflict risk noted for O2.
alternatives_considered: Free-form plugin execution with user-defined ordering only
Event-bus style hooks without phase boundaries
Fully parallel plugin execution
what_would_change_this_decision: If performance needs demand parallelism at large scales (Q3), selective parallel stages could be introduced with stricter immutability constraints.
If users require highly customized pipelines, a more flexible event-bus model might be needed (at the cost of determinism).

evidence_pointers.note: O2 interface list implies structured hook phases (ingest/transform/render/emit).
K20 highlights non-deterministic build risks that deterministic ordering mitigates.

decision_log.question: What is the canonical identifier for notes in the shared build context to avoid collisions and enable stable linking/backlinks?
decision_log.choice: Use a normalized, source-root-relative path-based NoteId as canonical (with a separate display title field).
decision_log.rationale: Path-based identity avoids collisions from duplicate titles or common filenames (e.g., multiple index.md) and provides stable resolution targets for link/backlink computation, directly addressing collision and graph-integrity risks.
alternatives_considered: Title-based slugs as the primary identifier
Content-hash identifiers
User-specified explicit IDs in front matter
what_would_change_this_decision: If users require URL slugs independent of paths, a secondary slug mapping can be introduced while keeping NoteId path-based internally.
If the repository structure is unstable or frequently reorganized, explicit front-matter IDs may become necessary.

evidence_pointers.note: K10 describes collisions/overwrites; path-based canonical IDs mitigate this.
K9 highlights backlink correctness edge cases; canonical IDs reduce ambiguity.

decision_log.question: What internal link conventions are supported by default, and how are unresolved links handled?
decision_log.choice: Default support: standard Markdown relative links to other Markdown notes (R9). Unresolved internal links emit build-time warnings (R18) and render as clearly non-navigable by default; add optional strict mode to fail builds on unresolved links.
decision_log.rationale: This satisfies the MUST baseline (R9) without overcommitting to additional syntaxes before Q1 is resolved, while still providing author feedback and preventing silent navigation defects.
alternatives_considered: Support wiki-links (e.g., [[Title]]) by default
Fail the build by default on any unresolved link
Silently render broken links without warnings
what_would_change_this_decision: If Q1 confirms wiki-links are required for the primary dataset, enable them by default (or provide an auto-detect mode with clear precedence rules).
If the system is primarily used in CI for publishing, default strictness could be increased to fail on unresolved links.

evidence_pointers.note: R9 requires correct resolution of standard Markdown relative links.
R18 (SHOULD) specifies warning-not-fail behavior for unresolved links by default.
Q1 is a blocking question on supported link conventions.

decision_log.question: What tag extraction conventions and normalization rules are supported initially?
decision_log.choice: Initial supported convention: YAML front matter tags (configurable field name) with normalization (trim + lowercase) enabled by default; allow extension to inline hashtags as a later plugin enhancement.
decision_log.rationale: This meets the MUST requirement to support at least one configurable convention (R11) while reducing ambiguity until Q2 is resolved, and it mitigates tag inconsistency risk (K3) by enforcing a single normalization pipeline.
alternatives_considered: Inline hashtags (#tag) as the only initial convention
Support both YAML and inline by default with heuristic merging
No normalization (preserve raw tags as-is)
what_would_change_this_decision: If Q2 confirms inline hashtags are dominant in the user’s notes, prioritize inline parsing and define precedence/merging rules with front matter.
If users require case-sensitive tags, make normalization opt-in with a clear migration path.

evidence_pointers.note: R11 requires tag extraction from at least one user-selectable/configurable convention.
R16 (SHOULD) encourages configurable tag normalization rules.
K3 describes undefined/inconsistent tag extraction; normalization mitigates.
Q2 is a blocking question on tag specification and normalization.

decision_log.question: How will client-side search indexing be implemented to satisfy static hosting constraints while managing scale/performance risk?
decision_log.choice: Generate a build-time, static search index artifact (JSON or equivalent) and perform all queries in-browser; implement size/performance reporting and design for optional chunking/lazy-loading if Q3 indicates larger scale.
decision_log.rationale: This directly satisfies R7/R8 and aligns with the static-only constraint. The performance risks (K4/K5) are managed by making scale a first-class input (Q3) and by designing the index format for evolvability (chunking) without changing the rest of the pipeline.
alternatives_considered: Rely on server-side search (rejected by constraints/non-goals)
Ship a single monolithic index without reporting or budgets
Defer search until late without early artifact decisions
what_would_change_this_decision: If Q3 indicates very large corpora, consider more aggressive index compression and chunking strategies and tighter performance budgets.
If the user prioritizes simplest implementation over performance, accept a basic index with documented limits.

evidence_pointers.note: R7 requires client-side search fully in-browser.
R8 requires build-time generation/shipping of a search index artifact.
K4 covers scale-related build failure (slow/crash).
K5 covers client-side index size/performance degradation.
Q3 is blocking for choosing indexing/performance targets.

decision_log.question: What is the default security boundary for rendering note content (raw HTML, escaping, and injection risks)?
decision_log.choice: Default to disallowing raw HTML in Markdown rendering (or sanitizing it), and enforce escaping of all user-controlled strings in templates; document the trust model explicitly.
decision_log.rationale: Rendering arbitrary note content into a static site that runs in browsers creates XSS risk (K7). A safe-by-default renderer and strict template escaping reduce exposure for both personal and shared publishing scenarios.
alternatives_considered: Allow raw HTML by default for maximum fidelity
Allow raw HTML but only warn
Rely solely on user trust and do no sanitization/escaping
what_would_change_this_decision: If the user explicitly requires raw HTML support for key notes and accepts the risk, move to an opt-in flag with strong warnings and documented consequences.
If a vetted sanitization strategy is approved, allow a limited safe subset of HTML.

evidence_pointers.note: K7 describes XSS/content injection risk in rendered pages.

decision_log.question: How will the build prevent accidental publication of private/sensitive notes (K8) given static hosting and no access control?
decision_log.choice: Implement a mandatory build-time privacy safeguard: notes marked private (e.g., front matter flag) are excluded from output and search index by default, and the build fails unless the user explicitly acknowledges an override flag; emit a report listing excluded private notes.
decision_log.rationale: K8 is critical and cannot be mitigated at runtime in a static site. A build-time, safe-by-default exclusion plus an explicit acknowledgment step reduces accidental leakage risk while still allowing intentional publishing if the user truly wants it.
alternatives_considered: No safeguard (rely on user awareness only)
Only warn but still publish private-marked notes
Always fail the build if any private-marked note exists (no override)
what_would_change_this_decision: If the user’s workflow is exclusively private/local hosting, the failure-on-private default may be relaxed to warnings while keeping exclusion behavior.
If the user needs multiple privacy categories, expand to allowlists/denylists and more granular policies (with corresponding UX/documentation).

evidence_pointers.note: K8 is the critical privacy leakage risk requiring build-time mitigation.

decision_log.question: How will build outputs be kept deterministic to support reliable publishing workflows?
decision_log.choice: Enforce deterministic ordering for discovery, tag lists, link lists, and emitted pages; avoid embedding timestamps by default; standardize locale/timezone behaviors for any formatting.
decision_log.rationale: Deterministic builds reduce noisy diffs and improve reproducibility (K20), and they are especially important in a plugin-based pipeline where multiple plugins may touch shared output ordering.
alternatives_considered: Allow OS/filesystem ordering (non-deterministic)
Embed build timestamps for traceability
Only partially sort some outputs (e.g., notes but not tags/links)
what_would_change_this_decision: If users require build metadata, provide an optional manifest with timestamps rather than embedding timestamps into pages/content.
If performance becomes an issue at scale, apply sorting only where user-visible and keep internal structures optimized.

evidence_pointers.note: K20 explicitly calls out non-deterministic builds and recommends deterministic ordering and avoiding timestamps.

supplemental_evaluations.title: Requirements-to-architecture coverage (core MUST set)
supplemental_evaluations.notes: O2’s separation into ingestion, transform (tags/links), render, search, and emit plugins provides a direct mapping to MUST requirements: R1/R5/R6 (CLI+ingestion), R2/R14 (static output + browser compatibility), R3/R4 (Markdown parsing/rendering), R9/R10 (links/backlinks plugin), R11–R13 (tags plugin + pages), and R7/R8 (search index + client-side runtime). This supports staged delivery while keeping acceptance testing attributable per plugin and per lifecycle phase.

evidence.note: O2 enumerates plugins for ingestion, metadata/tags, links/backlinks, render, theme/templates, search, and emit.
MUST requirements span ingestion, rendering, linking/backlinks, tags, search, and static output.

synthesis_warnings.summary: Blocking open questions (Q1/Q2/Q3/Q4/Q10) remain unanswered and can materially change link parsing, tag extraction, search approach/performance budgets, site IA/navigation, and distribution/UX decisions. This plan includes safe defaults, but HITL confirmation is needed before locking implementation details.

evidence.note: Linking conventions are blocking and affect link/backlink plugin design.
Tag conventions/normalization are blocking and affect tag plugin behavior.
Scale requirements are blocking for search/indexing and performance targets.
Information architecture requirements are blocking for templates/navigation.
CLI/GUI/build-integration expectation is blocking for product shape and UX.

synthesis_warnings.summary: Security boundary decision (raw HTML handling and template escaping) requires explicit trust-model approval per governance policy, because it impacts XSS exposure for any published site.

evidence.note: K7 is a high-severity XSS/content injection risk tied to rendering and templating.

synthesis_warnings.summary: Critical privacy leakage risk (K8) requires an explicit product decision on default behavior (exclude + fail build vs warn vs allow) and user experience for acknowledging overrides; proceed only with HITL approval.

evidence.note: K8 is critical and has no runtime mitigation under static hosting constraints.
